newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Gloves off in Creditanstalt race.
newsitem.headline: Gloves off in Creditanstalt race.

text.p: Battle lines were drawn in the sale of Austria's flagship bank Creditanstalt on Thursday as an EA-Generali-led group set about finalising its bid and considered the emergence of Bank Austria as a rival.

The so-called "Austrian consortium", representing a ragbag of financial and industrial interests, will have to raise its offer if it wants to take up the gauntlet thrown down at the eleventh hour by market leader Bank Austria.
Final bids for Creditanstalt, once banker to the Habsburg rulers of the Austro-Hungarian empire, have to land on Finance Minister Viktor Klima's desk by Monday.
"The consortium will meet during the afternoon to formulate its final, firm bid and discuss the current situation," a spokesman for Italian-controlled EA-Generali said.
EA-Generali shares slumped 9.12 percent to 3,090 schillings in Vienna as investors sensed the firm's chances of buying into the nation's number two bank were fading.
"People are worried EA-Generali may also miss out on existing insurance business with Creditanstalt," a trader said.
Bank Austria, controlled by the City of Vienna, is reportedly willing to pay 16 billion schillings ($1.47 billion) for a majority stake in its arch rival.

That works out at 804 schillings for each of the state's 19.9 million ordinary shares, representing 70 percent of ordinary voting stock, and is substantially above the 720-730 schillings the EA-Generali group has put up.
Creditanstalt ordinaries were up 1.7 percent at 732 in midday trading in Vienna.
Creditanstalt workers' council, sensing imminent job cuts, vowed to fight a union with Bank Austria and called a protest meeting for Friday.
"We want to protest against this..elephant's marriage," workers' council head Helmut Wasser said.
Creditanstalt management too has baulked at what it considers an aggressive takeover by another state-owned firm and a political rival.
Bank Austria is a stronghold of the ruling Social Democrats while Creditanstalt is a close ally of junior, conservative coalition partner the People's Party.
"This is not a privatisation but under the guise of a privatisation will polarise the whole sector," said one executive, talking on condition of anonymity.

Creditanstalt and conservatives in the government have publicly backed the EA-Generali group, which includes "conservative" savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse, Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commerciale Italiana.
Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky and People's Party leader Wolfgang Schuessel trod carefully through the political minefield on Thursday, however.
Vranitzky said the emergence of a second bidder gave the finance ministry more room to manoeuvre but added: "It is always better to find a joint solution."
Schuessel declined all comment.

The nation's two biggest banks would have combined assets of over 1,300 billion schillings, putting the "Austrian giant" in the top 30 of European banks and giving it 25 percent of the notoriously overcrowded domestic banking sector.
($1=10.86 Schilling)
